title: The LORD Comes Down
sum: The book opens with its own heading: the word of the LORD came to Micah of Moresheth in the days of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, "about Samaria and Jerusalem." Then the LORD is called as a witness against all the peoples. He leaves his place, comes down, and the mountains melt under his feet. The reason is named at once: Jacob's rebellion. Where does it come from? Samaria, the northern capital. And Judah's high places? Jerusalem. Samaria will be a heap of rubble, ready for planting vines, and its idols and wages will be burned.

The prophet's own voice breaks in at verse 8. He will mourn and howl, because Samaria's wound has come to Judah and touched the gate of Jerusalem. The rest of the chapter is a lament made of puns: a run of town names in the low hills of the Shephelah, each given a line that plays on its sound. In Gath, do not tell it. In Beth-leaphrah, roll in the dust. Lachish, hitch up the horses. Moresheth-gath, Micah's own home, is handed over like a bride. The chapter ends with a woman shaving her head in grief for children who are going into exile.
readings: Read as warning before 722

Chapter 1 is Micah's first message, spoken in Ahaz's reign while Samaria still stands (1:6). The lament in 1:8-16 comes later, as the Assyrian threat reaches Judah's border towns. The towns are named in the order a traveler would meet them. The point is a warning to Jerusalem: what is about to happen to Samaria will reach you.
Read as the campaign of 701 BC

The town list matches the area Sennacherib attacked in 701 BC: Lachish, Mareshah, Moresheth-gath, Gath and the Shephelah towns fell before he turned to Jerusalem (2 Kings 18:13-17). Verse 9, where the wound "touches the gate" of Jerusalem, then describes the siege itself. Most commentators prefer this.
Read as a prophetic poem, not a map

The towns are named for their sounds, not for a route. Not every town was attacked; the puns serve the lament, and the list is a work of art. The "you" of verses 11 to 16 shifts between a town, Daughter Zion and Judah's rulers. The poem teaches that every town, even one named "Pleasant", is within reach of the LORD's judgment.

views.H: Samaria fell in 722/721 BC after a three-year Assyrian siege (2 Kings 17:5-6). Sennacherib came into Judah in 701, took Lachish and, by his own account, 46 walled cities, and shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem "like a bird in a cage" (the Taylor Prism). The towns of 1:10-16 are in the Shephelah, the zone he attacked first. Micah's own village, Moresheth-gath, lay in it. The Lachish reliefs from Sennacherib's palace at Nineveh show the siege ramp and the deportation of its people, which fits 1:16.
views.C: Verses 2-7 are usually dated before 722; 1:8-16 are usually dated to the crisis of 701 or earlier raids. The Hebrew of 1:10-16 is among the hardest in the prophets: the Greek translation differs greatly, and several verses (1:11-12) are unclear in the Hebrew itself. Some critics think the speeches in 1:2-7 and 1:8-16 were joined by an editor; others see one poem. The first superscription may have been added when the book was assembled.
views.J: Jewish tradition counts the book among the Twelve, said in Bava Batra 15a to have been written by the Men of the Great Assembly. Jeremiah's elders remember Micah as Hezekiah's prophet (Jeremiah 26:18). Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak comment on the book in the Rabbinic Bible. The best-known synagogue uses of Micah are the haftarot from chapters 5 and 7, treated in the other part of this book.
views.X: Christian readers have taken 1:2-7 as a lesson that Jerusalem is no safer than Samaria. Jerome, Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret and Cyril of Alexandria each wrote a commentary on the Twelve that includes Micah. Matthew 11:21-24 has a similar pattern, in which towns that heard the most are judged most strictly.
views.F: Most readers take the chapter to be fulfilled in 722 and 701 and to say nothing of the end. The picture of the LORD coming down so that mountains melt (1:3-4) is in the poetry that other prophets use for the day of the LORD (Isaiah 64:1-3; Nahum 1:5), and some readers connect it to the last judgment. The chapter itself names no end-time event.

deep.b:
Micah plays on the sound of each town's name. The Plain keeps the Hebrew names and gives the meaning in the glosses. The list, in the order of the verses:

  • Gath (Gat) sounds like taggidu, "tell". Compare David's lament over Saul (2 Samuel 1:20).
  • Beth-leaphrah (Bet le'afrah) is "house of dust"; the command is to roll in 'afar, dust.
  • Shaphir (Shapir) means "pleasant"; its people go off naked and ashamed.
  • Zaanan (Tsa'anan) sounds like yatsa', "go out"; the people do not come out.
  • Beth-ezel is "house of the side" or "next-door house"; its mourning takes away the neighbor's foothold.
  • Maroth (Marot) means "bitter things"; its people hope for good.
  • Lachish (Lakhish) sounds like rekhesh, a team of swift horses.
  • Moresheth-gath sounds like me'orasah, "betrothed"; it is given as a parting gift.
  • Achzib (Akhziv) sounds like akhzav, "deceptive", a stream that dries up.
  • Mareshah (Mareshah) sounds like yoresh, "one who takes possession".
  • Adullam is where David hid, and where the glory of Israel will go.

Most of these lie in the Shephelah. Moresheth is probably Tell el-Judeideh (Tel Goded), Mareshah is Tel Maresha, Lachish is Tell ed-Duweir, Adullam is in the Elah valley. Gath, Shaphir, Beth-leaphrah, Beth-ezel and Maroth are less certain. The Greek text of this section shows how hard it was: it reads Beth-leaphrah as "laughingstock", Zaanan as "Senaar", and "inheritance" for Moresheth (see the variants).

Three kinds of evidence meet here. The Bible (2 Kings 18:13-19:36; Isaiah 36-37) says Sennacherib took the fortified cities of Judah, camped at Lachish and sent a force to Jerusalem; Hezekiah paid tribute (2 Kings 18:14). Sennacherib's own annals (the Taylor Prism, in the British Museum) say he shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem "like a bird in a cage", took 46 walled cities, and carried off 200,150 people. And the large relief from his palace at Nineveh, now in the British Museum, shows the siege and capture of Lachish; Ussishkin's excavations at Tell ed-Duweir found the Assyrian siege ramp and the destruction of the Judean city. None of these names Micah, and the Bible does not date 1:10-16 to 701. But the fit is close enough that most commentators read the poem as the lament of that year.

deep.title: Claude's theory: a lament for the prophet's own countryside
deep.b: Micah comes from Moresheth-gath, and the poem moves among the towns around it. My theory is that the section is more than clever puns: it is the grief of a country man for his neighbors. The prophet says "I will mourn" (1:8) before he names a single town, and the last town he names before the end is his own, "given away" (1:14). On this reading the mourning gestures of verse 8 are not a performance for the capital but the real grief of a man who knows the people he is announcing judgment on. This overlaps with commentators who stress Micah's rural origin and the personal tone of the lament (Mays, Wolff), but the connection between the verb "I will mourn" and the choice of his own town as the last in the list is my own reading.

echoes: 1 Kings 22:28; Deuteronomy 32:1; Judges 5:4-5; Psalm 18:7-15; Amos 1:2; Hosea 9:1; 2 Samuel 1:20; 2 Kings 17:5-6; 2 Kings 18:13-17; Jeremiah 15:18; Isaiah 8:7-8

settings.by: Not stated; the heading says it records the LORD's word to Micah
settings.to: Readers and hearers of the book, in Judah
settings.when: Probably after the events, since it names three reigns
settings.why: To tell the reader that what follows is a word received, dated to three kings of Judah, and about both capitals.
views: Traditional view: the prophet himself wrote the heading and the book.
The heading speaks of Micah in the third person and spans three reigns; many critics think an editor added it when the collection was made, perhaps after the exile.

settings.to: All the peoples as witnesses; first of all Israel and Judah, who hear it as a warning
settings.when: Before Samaria's fall in 722/721 BC (1:6), in the days of Ahaz or earlier, in the speaker's own time
settings.why: To announce that Samaria's ruin is the LORD's act and is caused by its idols and wealth, and to tell Jerusalem, which hears it, that the same charge applies to it (1:5).
views: The predictions are in the future tense and look forward to Samaria's destruction. Most commentators place the speech before the fall.
Some think the verses were reshaped after the fall; the picture of the ruin and the burned images fits what happened.

settings.what: Lament over the towns of the Shephelah
settings.to: The people of Judah, in particular those in the foothill towns named, and Jerusalem
settings.when: As the Assyrian army approaches Judah; most commentators say 701 BC, others an earlier raid
settings.why: To make Judah see the danger by naming their own towns, and to show that the prophet shares their grief. The poem asks them to begin the mourning before the disaster.
views: The Assyrian invasion under Sennacherib (the commonest view).
Some date it to the Assyrian-Philistine campaigns of Sargon II (about 713 to 711 BC) or to the Syro-Ephraimite war, since the poem never names Sennacherib.

title: The Land-Grabbers
sum: Woe to those who lie awake planning harm, and carry it out at dawn because they have the power. Their crime is plain: they crave fields and take them, crave houses and take them, and crush a man and his household and the land he inherited. The LORD answers with a plan of his own, a disaster they cannot slip out from under, and a taunt song in which their own ruin is sung back at them. When they do not hold the land, they will have no one to measure out a share in the LORD's assembly.

Then the opponents speak: "Do not rant." Micah answers that they have driven women out of their homes and taken the honor of children, and that the people want a prophet full of wind and beer. The chapter ends on an unexpected turn. The LORD will gather all of Jacob, the remnant of Israel, like sheep in an enclosure. The one who breaks through goes ahead, the king goes in front, and the LORD is at their head. Whether these two verses promise rescue or threaten siege has been argued for centuries.
readings: Read as an accusation of land theft

Verses 1-5 and 8-10 name specific acts: seizing fields and houses, stripping coats, putting widows out. The prophet speaks for farmers who were losing the land that the law said was God's gift to each family. The language of covetousness comes from the Ten Commandments.
Read as a debate about preaching

Verses 6-7 and 11 show Micah arguing with people who tell him to stop prophesying and want a prophet of wine and beer. The chapter is a case study of the conflict between true and false prophecy that runs through the book (3:5-8).
Read verses 12-13 as hope, or as threat

As hope: the LORD gathers the survivors and leads them out through the breach, like a shepherd and king. As threat: the flock is penned in a besieged city, and the "breaker" is the enemy or the LORD breaking down the walls. Both can be read without changing the Hebrew.

views.H: In the late 700s BC debt, royal land grants and fines were moving farms from small families to officials in Judah. Isaiah (Isaiah 5:8) and Amos (Amos 2:6-8) describe the same thing. The text does not name the men; commentators think of the royal officials and landowners in Jerusalem and the Shephelah. The "clan" of 2:3 is the whole people. The threat of removal fits the Assyrian deportations after 722 and 701.
views.C: Verses 12-13 are widely thought to be a later addition: commentators such as Wolff and Mays regard them as later, from the time of the exile (check their commentaries at 2:12-13), and Waltke defends them as Micah's own. The speakers in 2:6-11 are hard to separate; Hebrew gives no quotation marks, and scholars argue where the opponents' words end and Micah's begin (2:6, 7, 11). The text of 2:8-9 is among the hardest in the book.
views.J: Rashi, Radak and the Targum comment on 2:12-13, the one place in the chapter that Jewish commentators read at length; their wording has not been checked for this scroll, so no Jewish reading of the breaker is reported here. Jewish tradition counts "do not covet" among the commandments (Maimonides lists it in the Sefer HaMitzvot), and the laws of the Jubilee (Leviticus 25) protect family land. These are the background against which the prophet is read. In the Talmud's account of the 613 commandments (Makkot 23b-24a), Micah is the prophet who reduces them to three (Micah 6:8, in the other part of this book).
views.X: Jesus condemns scribes who "eat up widows' houses" (Luke 20:47), the same offense. James 5:1-6 charges the rich with holding back the wages of those who cut their fields. Jerome is reported in later commentaries to have read 2:12-13 as the church gathered by Christ, the "breaker" who goes ahead of his people (his own commentary has not been checked for this scroll). The Greek of 2:13 reads "through the breach", with no person called the breaker.
views.F: Verses 12-13 are read as a promise of the final gathering of Israel under the LORD as king. Jewish and Christian readers who expect a restoration of Israel to its land, and those who read it as the gathering of the church, both use the verses. The passage names no date.

deep.b: In Israel's law the land belongs to the LORD: "The land must not be sold for good, because the land is mine" (Leviticus 25:23). Each family received a share at the conquest, and the share was not to leave the family (Numbers 36:7). A man who fell into debt could sell it only until the next Jubilee (Leviticus 25:10-28), and a kinsman was to buy it back. Boundaries were protected by a curse (Deuteronomy 19:14; 27:17). The story of Naboth shows what happened when a king wanted a family's field (1 Kings 21:1-16). Micah's complaint is that, in his day, the legal means for taking land had become a way to steal it. He does not accuse the rich of breaking the law as written, but of using power to turn the law against its purpose. The sin is twofold: craving (the commandment) and taking (the act). That is why the LORD's answer is that no one will measure out a share for them in the LORD's assembly (2:5).
deep.refs: Leviticus 25:23; Numbers 36:7; Deuteronomy 19:14; 1 Kings 21:1-16; Isaiah 5:8; Amos 2:6-8

deep.b: Hebrew has no quotation marks, so the voices must be worked out from grammar and sense. The Plain reads it this way. In 2:6 the opponents speak ("Do not rant"). In 2:7 Micah (or the LORD) answers with a question and a defense: do my words not do good for the honest? In 2:8-10 the prophet accuses and gives the LORD's order to go. In 2:11 he returns to the opponents with a sneer. Other readings make 2:7a the opponents' words ("Is the Spirit of the LORD cut short?" is their argument that the LORD would never punish), and some make 2:6 the words of the false prophets and not the rich. The shifting voices are part of the point: this is a dispute, and the chapter lets the other side speak.

echoes: Exodus 20:17; Deuteronomy 5:21; Leviticus 25:23; Numbers 36:7; 1 Kings 21; Isaiah 5:8; Amos 2:6-8; Amos 7:16; Deuteronomy 12:9; Exodus 13:21; Isaiah 52:12; Luke 20:47

settings.to: The officials and landowners of Judah who seized family land
settings.when: In the later 700s BC, while the powerful of Judah were taking land (the text gives no date)
settings.why: To tell them that the LORD sees what is done on beds at night and carried out by day, and will answer with a plan of his own; to warn them that they will have no share when the land is divided again.
views: The disaster is the Assyrian invasion and deportation, which will leave the families without land (2:4-5).
A threat of judgment at the LORD's assembly
The loss of a place in the LORD's assembly (2:5) is read as exclusion from the covenant people.

settings.to: The people of Judah, and the opponents who told Micah not to prophesy
settings.when: At the time of the land seizures, in the public square or at the gate
settings.why: To answer those who say the LORD would never be so harsh, and to expose their own acts: robbing passers-by, driving out women and children. The people want a comfortable prophet, and Micah says so.
views: The speakers who say "Do not rant" are the landowners.
The speakers are rival prophets of peace, as in 3:5 (a view found in several commentaries).

settings.to: Jacob and the remnant of Israel; the exiles, on the usual reading
settings.when: Debated: the days of Micah, or the exile, when a later editor placed it here
settings.why: To promise that the LORD will gather the survivors and lead them out; or, on the minority reading, to threaten a siege. The effect in the book is to put a promise right after the threats, and to start the pattern of judgment and hope that the book repeats.
views: Salvation in the time of the exile
A promise added to the book after 586 BC (commentators such as Wolff and Mays; check their commentaries at 2:12-13).
A promise given in the crisis of 701 BC, when Jerusalem was spared (for example Waltke).
A threat of siege: the sheep are penned in the city (no commentator is named here; the Greek "in distress" at 2:12 supports it).

title: Hear, You Rulers
sum: A second "Hear." Micah turns on the heads and rulers of Israel, who ought to know justice and instead hate good and love evil. He uses the language of a butcher shop: they rip the skin off the people, break their bones, and chop them up like meat for the pot. When they cry to the LORD, he will not answer. The prophets who lead the people astray come next. They shout "Peace!" for anyone who feeds them and declare holy war on anyone who does not. For them night will fall: no vision, no answer.

Micah sets himself against them. He is full of strength, with the LORD's Spirit, justice and might, to tell Jacob his rebellion. Then the rulers are addressed again: they build Zion with blood. Judges take bribes, priests teach for a fee, prophets divine for silver, and all of them lean on the LORD and say that no harm can come to them. The chapter ends with the sentence Jeremiah's elders quote about a hundred years later: because of you, Zion will be plowed like a field, Jerusalem will be heaps of rubble, and the mountain of the house will be high ground in a forest.
readings: Read as a charge against the three offices

Chiefs, priests and prophets are the three offices of Deuteronomy 16-18. Each has been bought: judges by bribes, priests by fees, prophets by silver (3:11). The chapter lists what has gone wrong with every office that was meant to guard justice, teaching and vision.
Read as a contrast of two prophets

The chapter sets the prophets who say what is paid for (3:5-7) against the one who says what is true (3:8). Micah's claim to the Spirit is the answer to the "wind" of 2:11. It lets the reader judge the test of a prophet by what the message costs him.
Read as the book's turning point

Verse 12 is the sentence of death for Jerusalem, and chapters 4-5 start with the opposite: the mountain of the LORD's house, high above all hills. The book's structure puts the two pictures of the same mountain side by side.

views.H: Hezekiah's reign saw both a reform (2 Kings 18:4) and the threat of Sennacherib (701). Jeremiah 26:19 says Hezekiah did not put Micah to death but feared the LORD and sought his favor, and that the LORD changed his mind about the harm. The verse about the plowed field was understood about a hundred years later as having helped bring about a reform. Jerusalem was spared in 701 (2 Kings 19:35-36) and fell in 586.
views.C: Chapter 3 is the part of Micah that most scholars attribute to the prophet himself. The Hebrew is clearer than in chapter 1. Some critics think 3:8 ("with the Spirit of the LORD") is a later gloss; no manuscript lacks it. Jeremiah 26:18 shows that 3:12 was known in Jerusalem by the late 7th century, which sets a firm latest date for the verse.
views.J: The Talmud (Makkot 24b) tells how Rabban Gamaliel, Rabbi Eleazar ben Azariah, Rabbi Joshua and Rabbi Akiva saw foxes coming out of the place of the Holy of Holies after the destruction. Three wept; Akiva laughed, because Micah 3:12's prophecy of Zion plowed like a field had come true, and so the promise of its restoration (Zechariah 8:4) would also come true. The Mishnah (Ta'anit 4:6) lists the plowing up of the city among the calamities of the Ninth of Av.
views.X: Jesus says that not one stone of the Temple will be left on another (Matthew 24:2), the same sentence. Christian readers have connected the fall of the Temple in AD 70 with Jesus' words, and have often applied Micah's attack on paid priests and prophets to the church's own leaders.
views.F: Zion plowed like a field is read as fulfilled in 586 BC and AD 70 (and the plowing of Jerusalem after AD 135 in some accounts). Readers who expect a rebuilt Temple in the last days see the reverse picture in 4:1; readers who see the church as the new temple read it as already true.

deep.b: About a hundred years after Micah, Jeremiah stood in the Temple court and said that the Temple would become like Shiloh (Jeremiah 26:6). The priests and prophets demanded his death. Some elders then stood up and quoted Micah: "Zion will be plowed like a field. Jerusalem will be heaps of rubble, and the mountain of the house will be high ground in a forest" (Jeremiah 26:18). They asked: did Hezekiah kill him? No. He feared the LORD, begged for mercy, and "the LORD changed his mind about the harm" (Jeremiah 26:19). The Hebrew of Micah 3:12 and Jeremiah 26:18 is word for word the same, so this Plain gives them in the same English. The elders' argument is that a prophet who spoke the same sentence in the same city was heard, and that repentance, not execution, was the right response. It is among the clearest cases in the Bible of one prophet's words being quoted by name and date. It also shows that Micah's threat did not fail when the city survived in 701: the elders say it was turned aside by repentance, as Jeremiah 18:7-10 teaches. The same Jeremiah passage mentions a prophet, Uriah, who spoke like Jeremiah and was killed (Jeremiah 26:20-23).

Few of the writing prophets before the exile say that the Spirit of the LORD empowers them. Hosea 9:7 reports the other side: "the man of the spirit is mad." Micah answers by claiming it, in a verse that sets the Spirit beside justice and might, the qualities the rulers lack (3:1, 9). In Hebrew the claim is about equipment for a task: he is full of strength "to declare to Jacob his rebellion." The verse gave later readers a way to say what a prophet is: a person made strong by the Spirit to name sin. Compare Isaiah 61:1 and Ezekiel 2:2. Christian readers have linked it to the gift of the Spirit at Pentecost (Acts 2); Jewish readers to the rabbinic teaching that prophecy came through the Holy Spirit.

echoes: Jeremiah 26:17-19; Jeremiah 7:4; Jeremiah 6:14; Ezekiel 13:10; Ezekiel 11:3; Psalm 14:4; Habakkuk 2:12; Amos 5:15; Proverbs 1:28; Exodus 23:8; Deuteronomy 16:19; Isaiah 1:23; Hosea 9:7; Matthew 24:2

settings.to: The heads of Jacob and rulers of the house of Israel: the judges and administrators of Judah and Jerusalem
settings.when: In Hezekiah's reign or earlier, at the gate or at court (the text gives no date)
settings.why: To tell the men in charge that they know what justice is and still ruin the people they serve, and that when they cry for help the LORD will not answer. The "Hear" marks a formal address.
views: The leaders are the royal officials and elders of Jerusalem.
Because "Jacob" and "Israel" can name the northern kingdom, some think the speech was first for the leaders of Samaria and later applied to Jerusalem.

settings.what: Speech against the prophets, and Micah's own claim
settings.to: The prophets who proclaim peace, and the people who pay them
settings.when: In the same period, in the same public setting
settings.why: To say that prophets who say what the payer wants will lose their vision, and to mark the difference with Micah, who has the Spirit and tells the truth. It lets the hearers decide whom to believe.
views: The prophets are officials attached to the king and Temple, as in 1 Kings 22.
They are traveling prophets who lived on the gifts of the people (as 3:5 says).

settings.what: Second speech to the rulers; Zion plowed
settings.to: The heads and rulers again, and all who trusted that the LORD was in Zion
settings.when: The days of Hezekiah, as Jeremiah's elders recall (Jeremiah 26:18), if their report is accurate
settings.why: To say that Jerusalem's confidence that "the LORD is among us" is false while the city is built on blood, and to announce its fall in the plainest terms. It was remembered about a hundred years later as the threat that moved the king to seek the LORD.
views: Jeremiah 26:19 reads it as a warning heeded by Hezekiah, so the threat was lifted.
The Temple fell in 586 BC; the sentence was delayed, not canceled.

title: The Mountain of the LORD
sum: The opposite picture to 3:12. In the days to come, the mountain where the LORD's house stands will be set firm at the head of the mountains, and peoples will run to it like a river. They say, "Let us climb the LORD's mountain." Teaching comes out of Zion and the LORD's word from Jerusalem. He judges between peoples and settles the disputes of mighty nations far away, and they pound their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning knives. Micah adds what Isaiah does not: each person will sit under their own vine and fig tree and no one will terrify them. The peoples still follow their gods, but "we will walk in the name of the LORD our God for ever and ever."

Then the scene returns to the present. The LORD will gather the lame and the outcast and make them a remnant, and he will be king on Mount Zion. But Daughter Zion cries out in labor pains: she must leave the city, camp in the open, and go as far as Babylon, where the LORD will redeem her. Many nations gather to see her defiled, not knowing that the LORD has gathered them like grain for the threshing floor. Zion is told to get up and thresh, with an iron horn and bronze hooves, and to give the nations' stolen wealth to the Lord of all the earth. A note on numbering: the Hebrew Bible's chapter 4 has 14 verses, and its last verse is English 5:1 (see the note at 4:13); this site uses the English numbers.
readings: Read as the end of history

"In the days to come" is the end of this age. The nations come to Zion for good, war stops, and the LORD reigns there forever. Jews and Christians who read it this way disagree about whether Zion is the city, the people of God or the church.
Read as a promise Israel's prophets believed could come in history

The prophets' hope was that the nations would one day see what Israel had in the LORD, and the peace of 4:4 is the peace of Solomon's reign extended to everyone (1 Kings 4:25). It is hope, not a timetable.
Read as the book's answer to chapter 3

Chapter 3 says Zion will be plowed. Chapter 4 says the same mountain will be the highest. The book does not say how one becomes the other; it simply places both. The remnant, the lame and the outcasts are the way.

views.H: The peaceful vision is set against the history of the 8th and 7th centuries: Assyria's wars, the siege of 701, the exile to Babylon after 586. Hezekiah's Jerusalem was the one city that survived Sennacherib (2 Kings 19:35-36); 4:9-10 and 4:11-13 name the siege, the exile and the nations that gather against Zion. Babylon is mentioned in 4:10 as the place of exile, which was still about a hundred years in the future when Isaiah told Hezekiah the same (Isaiah 39:6).
views.C: 4:1-3 is the same oracle as Isaiah 2:2-4, with differences. The usual views are that one prophet quoted the other or that both used an older source. The date of 4:1-5 is debated: many critics place it after the exile, as an addition (for example Wolff and Mays); others defend it as the work of Micah (for example Waltke). The mention of Babylon in 4:10 is the main argument for an exilic date of 4:9-13 on the critical side.
views.J: Maimonides treats the end of war as part of the messianic age, when there will be no famine or war, no jealousy or competition (Laws of Kings 12:5). The Targum of the Minor Prophets, in the Cathcart and Gordon translation, is reported to read the "Tower of the Flock" of 4:8 as the Messiah of Israel, hidden because of the sins of the congregation of Zion (the Aramaic has not been checked for this scroll). Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak comment on 4:1-3, but their wording has not been read for this scroll and is not reported here.
views.X: The fathers read 4:1-3 as fulfilled in Christ: Justin (First Apology 39) and Irenaeus (Against Heresies 4.34.4) say the nations have laid down their swords and that Christians do not learn war. Origen draws on the passage in Against Celsus 5.33. Jerome is reported to read the mountain as the church. Calvin reads it as the spread of the gospel from Jerusalem (Luke 24:47; Acts 1:8). Christian traditions disagree about war and about whether the passage is fulfilled or future; see the cards.
views.F: The chapter is a main source of the picture of a future reign of the LORD from Zion. Dispensationalists (Walvoord, The Millennial Kingdom) read 4:1-8 as the thousand-year reign of Revelation 20, with a literal Jerusalem as the center. Reformed and amillennial readers read the same words of the church age and the new creation. The sculpture "Let Us Beat Swords into Plowshares" (Evgeniy Vuchetich, a gift of the Soviet Union in 1959) stands in the United Nations garden in New York, and Isaiah 2:4 is carved on the Isaiah Wall across the street.

deep.b:
The oracles are almost identical, but they differ in several details, and each difference is a clue. In Micah 4:1 the peoples "stream" 'alav (upon it) and the word is 'ammim (peoples); Isaiah has 'elav (to it) and kol-haggoyim (all the nations). In 4:2 Micah has "many nations" (goyim rabbim) where Isaiah has "many peoples" and adds "and up to" before the house of Jacob's God. In 4:3 Isaiah says the LORD will judge "between the nations" and set things right "for many peoples"; Micah says he will judge "between many peoples" and set things right "for mighty nations, however far away", words Isaiah lacks. In Micah the last verb has a final nun (yilmedun). Micah then adds 4:4-5; Isaiah follows with 2:5. Three explanations: Isaiah wrote first and Micah copied; Micah wrote first and Isaiah copied; both took the text from an older tradition, perhaps a temple hymn. Each commentator weighs the details (the added "mighty" and "far away" in Micah may be expansions, or the shorter Isaiah may be an abbreviation). The text is old enough to be quoted twice in the same century; the best summary is that nobody can be sure who gave it first.

The scrolls: 4Q82 (4QXIIg) preserves the start of Micah 4:1-2, and Mur88 preserves most of 4:1-3. They agree with the Masoretic Text, and in 4:1 both read 'alav 'ammim, "upon it, peoples", the Micah form. No scroll of Micah reads the Isaiah form.

Micah's name for the place of exile is a surprise. In the late 700s BC Babylon was a city under Assyrian rule, and the enemy that Micah's hearers feared was Assyria. Critical scholars therefore date 4:10, or the whole of 4:9-13, to the time after 586 BC, when Babylon had destroyed Jerusalem (for example Wolff and Mays). The reply of those who defend an early date is that Isaiah, in the same years, told Hezekiah that his house would be carried off to Babylon (Isaiah 39:6-7; 2 Kings 20:17-18), after Merodach-baladan's envoys visited, and that Merodach-baladan was an Assyrian-era rebel king of Babylon. The Hebrew says "you will go as far as Babylon", with no hint that Babylon is the destroyer; it is the place where the LORD rescues. Mur88 preserves 'ad Bavel, "as far as Babylon", and the Greek reads the same words, so there is no manuscript evidence that the word was added later.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the vine and fig tree answer the land-grabbers
deep.b: In chapter 2 the powerful crave fields and houses and take them from families, and the LORD says they will have no share. In 4:4 every person sits under their own vine and their own fig tree, and no one will terrify them. My theory is that this verse, which is not in Isaiah's version of the oracle, is Micah's own addition for this reason: it makes the vision of peace a vision in which the injustice of chapter 2 is undone. The nations stop war, and in the same breath everyone gets their own land. The verse repeats the Hebrew of 1 Kings 4:25 (Solomon's peace), so Micah borrows the idea of royal peace and gives it to every household. This overlaps with commentators who read 4:4 as the economic side of the peace (Mays and others), but the claim that the verse was added to answer chapter 2, and that Isaiah's version lacks it, is my own and cannot be proved.

echoes: Isaiah 2:2-5; Joel 3:10; 1 Kings 4:25; Zechariah 8:20-23; Zechariah 3:10; Psalm 46; Psalm 48; Isaiah 24:23; Isaiah 39:6; 2 Kings 20:17; Deuteronomy 25:4; Deuteronomy 33:17; 1 Kings 22:11; Luke 24:47; Acts 1:8

settings.to: The people of Judah and Jerusalem, hearing a promise after the sentence of 3:12
settings.when: Debated: the days of Hezekiah, or the exile and after
settings.why: To tell Judah that the mountain they were told would be plowed is the mountain to which the world will come for teaching, and that the peace the rulers failed to keep is the LORD's own gift in the end. The last verse (4:5) is the people's answer: whatever others do, we will walk in the LORD's name.
views: Waltke and others defend the oracle as part of Micah's message of hope.
Wolff and Mays, among others, treat 4:1-5 as an oracle from the time of the exile or later, placed beside Isaiah 2.
The oracle belongs to neither prophet but to an older Zion tradition both used.

settings.to: The weak and scattered of Israel, as the exiles or survivors
settings.when: "On that day": the future restoration; set by many in the exile
settings.why: To promise that the LORD will gather those he hurt, and that the weakest will be the nucleus of a strong nation under his kingship. It continues the theme of the remnant from 2:12.
views: The gathering is the return from Babylon.
The gathering is the end-time restoration of Israel.

settings.what: Zion in labor; the nations at the threshing floor
settings.to: Daughter Zion and Jerusalem, under siege
settings.when: The siege of Jerusalem: 701 BC on one view, 586 BC on another
settings.why: To give a city that thinks it has no king and no counselor a reason to endure: the pain is labor, the exile is a road to rescue, and the nations that gloat are on the LORD's threshing floor.
views: Micah speaks in Sennacherib's siege; Babylon is a foresight, as in Isaiah 39.
The verses are from the exile, and "Babylon" is the real place of exile.

traditions.q: Does "swords into plowshares" (4:3) mean Christians must not fight?
views: The Catechism calls earthly peace the image and fruit of the peace of Christ (2305). Those who renounce violence are witnesses to gospel love (2306), but governments have the right of lawful defense, under the strict conditions of a just war (2308-2309). These paragraphs state the church's teaching on peace and defense in general; they do not comment on Micah 4:3.

This entry is about war in general, not about this verse (for the Fathers' reading of Micah 4, see the next card). War is an evil and a result of the Fall, and the Church does not bless it as good. But it does not forbid the defense of neighbors. Basil's canonical letter said that those who had killed in war should abstain from communion for a time (Letter 188, canon 13). The Russian Orthodox Church's Social Concept (2000, chapter 8) teaches the same balance.

The Augsburg Confession (article 16) says that Christians may take part in just wars and serve as soldiers without sin. Luther separated the two kingdoms: the Christian does not fight for himself, but may serve in the office of the sword ("Whether Soldiers, Too, Can Be Saved").

Christian magistrates "may lawfully, now under the New Testament, wage war upon just and necessary occasion" (Westminster Confession 23.2). Calvin's teaching on just war is in Institutes 4.20.11-12. On Micah 4:1-3 his lectures read the passage as the spread of Christ's kingdom through the gospel to the nations (see the next card).
The Baptist Faith and Message (2000, article 16) says Christians should do all in their power to put an end to war, in the spirit of Christ. Baptists have held both pacifist and just-war views.

The Schleitheim Articles (1527, article 6) teach that the sword is ordained by God outside the perfection of Christ, and that the Christian follows Christ in not using it. The Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995, article 22) teaches nonresistance and active peacemaking.

Friends refuse all outward war on the ground of Christ's teaching. The declaration the Quakers presented to Charles II in 1660/61, written with George Fox, says they "utterly deny all outward wars and strife".

traditions.q: Who are the nations streaming to Zion in 4:1-5, and when?
views: The Fathers, whom Catholics and Orthodox both honor, read the passage as fulfilled when the nations came to Christ. Justin (First Apology 39) and Irenaeus (Against Heresies 4.34.4) say that the swords of the nations were already turned into plows by the gospel. Cyril of Alexandria and Theodoret of Cyrus read Micah 4 of Christ and the Church, from which the word went out beginning at Jerusalem. Jerome is reported to have read the mountain as the Church. Today the Second Vatican Council calls the Church the seed and beginning of Christ's kingdom on earth, which she awaits in its fullness (Lumen Gentium 5).

The Orthodox Church honors the same Fathers, among them Cyril of Alexandria and Theodoret of Cyrus, whose reading of Micah 4 is given in the entry above. This scroll has not found a separate Orthodox statement on the passage.

Article 17 of the Augsburg Confession rejects the opinion that, before the resurrection of the dead, the godly will take possession of the kingdom of the world while the ungodly are everywhere put down. It does not name Micah; it is the Lutheran confession's nearest statement to the earthly-kingdom reading described under Dispensationalist below.

Calvin takes the passage as the spread of Christ's kingdom through the gospel to all nations from Jerusalem, a work begun at Pentecost and not yet complete. Many Reformed amillennial and postmillennial writers follow him.

The Baptist Faith and Message (2000, article 10) confesses that Christ will return personally and visibly, that the dead will be raised and that Christ will judge, and it does not choose a view of the millennium. Baptists have held premillennial, amillennial and dispensational views, and so differ on this passage.

The passage describes a future thousand-year reign of Christ from a literal Jerusalem, when Israel is restored and the nations come to be taught (Walvoord, The Millennial Kingdom). The church age is a separate period. Historic premillennialists such as George Eldon Ladd also expect a future reign of Christ on earth, but part from the dispensationalists on the relation of Israel and the church (The Blessed Hope).
